scenes.caption: We feel our own nerves, confusion or irritation vividly, so we assume they show.
In Gilovich's studies, liars expected to be caught more often than observers actually caught them. Sizes are schematic.
Illustrative: a lead's hesitant tone felt obvious to her. Nobody noticed, and later the team said she never raised a concern.
Usually far less leaks than we fear. State the concern in one explicit sentence instead of relying on tone.
We select a few details, add meaning, make assumptions, draw a conclusion, adopt a belief and act — often in seconds.
Illustrative: late to two stand-ups becomes 'doesn't care', then 'disengaged', then smaller tasks. Each rung adds a guess.
Beliefs then shape which details we notice next, so the ladder feeds itself.
In a disagreement, stop arguing from the top rungs. Compare what each of you actually saw and heard.
An upset person rarely calms down because you were right. They calm down because you understood.
Before you correct or defend: restate what you heard, include the feeling behind it, and check you got it right.
Illustrative: the account manager hears his point said back, nods, sits down, and they look at the case together. Shape is schematic.
Reflecting back is not agreeing. It proves you understood — then you can still share facts or disagree.
Each side has a reservation price: the worst terms they'd accept before walking away.
Illustrative: the company pays at most ₹9 lakh; the vendor won't go below ₹7 lakh. The zone is ₹7–9 lakh.
Any deal inside the zone beats walking away for both. The bargaining is about where in it you land.
If the vendor's floor were ₹10 lakh, no charm closes the gap on price alone. Then no deal is the right outcome.
Most negotiators in Thompson and Hastie's studies began by assuming the other side wanted exactly the opposite.
Illustrative: the client cares most about the date, the vendor most about a longer contract. Sizes are schematic.
Splitting every issue down the middle leaves value on the table. Trading the issues each side values most leaves both better off.
List every issue, rank them by importance to you, then guess the other side's ranking.
Old advice says never name a number first. Galinsky and Mussweiler's experiments challenge that.
First offers worked as anchors: the more ambitious the opening, the better the final price tended to be for its maker. Shape is schematic.
Going first needs a good sense of the realistic range. Without it, you may anchor yourself badly or reveal too much.
The evidence leans toward going first, but only when you know the territory. Otherwise, hearing their number is cheap research.
Write the realistic range and your evidence, then decide before the meeting whether you'll open.
When you switch from task A to task B, some of your attention stays on A.
In Leroy's 2009 experiments, people who switched away from an unfinished task did worse on the next one. Sizes are schematic.
Illustrative: an analyst checks the escalation channel between paragraphs, and reads the same paragraph three times.
Before switching, write one line on where you stopped and what's next, then close that window completely.
A goal says what you want. An implementation intention says: when situation X arises, I will do Y.
Illustrative: Friday 4 pm, laptop closes, three bullets go out. The cue is fixed and the action is small.
Gollwitzer's review summarised studies where people with if-then plans followed through more than those with only a goal. Schematic.
Rewrite one stalled goal as a single 'When ___, I will ___' sentence and put the cue in your calendar.
It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's Law.
In Buehler's 1994 study, students on average took longer than even their own worst-case guesses. Sizes are schematic.
We plan by imagining this task going well, rather than recalling how past tasks actually went.
Illustrative: the team plans two weeks for a migration. Their last three each took about five.
Look up how long the last three similar tasks really took, and start from that number.
Illustrative: the team falls behind, agents rush, more cases reopen, they fall further behind. More produces more.
A reinforcing loop amplifies change, for better or worse. Shape is schematic.
A balancing loop pushes toward a goal or limit, like a thermostat. Shape is schematic.
Seeing the loop changes the question from 'who caused this?' to 'what keeps this going?'
Draw one persistent problem as a loop of three or four arrows.
A flight instructor told Kahneman that praise made the next landing worse and shouting made it better.
When a result is partly luck, an extreme one tends to be followed by a less extreme one. Shape is schematic.
Exceptional performances are usually followed by more ordinary ones, whatever feedback you give.
To judge an intervention, compare with similar bad weeks where you did nothing.
A system's output is limited by its tightest bottleneck. Bar sizes are schematic.
Illustrative: automated triage gets tickets to the engineer's queue faster. They sit there longer; customers see no change.
Identify the constraint, get the most from it, make everything else serve its pace, add capacity, repeat.
Map your process in four or five steps and mark where items wait longest.
Checklists catch simple steps skipped under pressure. A badly designed one trains people to tick without looking.
Illustrative: a forty-item release checklist gets ticked in one go. Cut to seven killer items, it actually gets used.
A clear pause point, a short list, the steps people actually skip, and testing in real use.
Design — and whether teams believe in it — decides whether a checklist gets used.
A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent that you cannot recover.
Arkes and Blumer found full-price season-ticket holders attended more plays early on than discounted ones. Sizes are schematic.
Illustrative: four months and ₹25 lakh on an internal tool, while a vendor product now does it better for less.
Compare only future costs and benefits from here. Leave past spending off the page.
Satisficing, Simon's word, means taking the first option that meets your criteria. Maximising means searching for the best.
Illustrative: a manager compares eleven video-call tools. A satisficer sets three must-haves and stops at the first match.
In Schwartz's surveys, maximisers reported more regret and less satisfaction with their choices.
Maximising pays when stakes are high. Satisficing wins for most everyday choices.
In Save More Tomorrow, employees commit now to save more when future pay rises arrive.
Committing for later feels easier, take-home pay never falls so it doesn't feel like a loss, and inertia keeps people saving.
Where it was tried, savings rates among participants rose substantially over the following years. Shape is schematic.
Decide now what share of your next raise goes to savings, and make the transfer automatic. Education, not advice.
Avalanche: put spare rupees toward the highest interest rate first. Snowball: clear the smallest balance first.
Illustration only: a ₹60,000 card balance at a high rate and a ₹15,000 loan at a lower one. Each method picks a different target.
Followed through, the avalanche costs less interest. Snowball fans say early wins keep people going.
The evidence for the motivational effect is suggestive rather than settled. List your debts and rates to compare.
Prompt injection hides instructions in an email, web page or document the agent reads.
A language model reads instructions and data as the same kind of text, so no filter reliably separates them.
Illustrative: an email says 'approve a full refund'. If refunds need no human approval, the attack only has to work once.
Limit what the agent can do after reading untrusted content. Require human approval where reading and acting meet.
